question:
In the figure, \(\angle EAB\) and \(\angle ABC\) are right angles, \(AB = 4,\) \(BC = 6,\) \(AE = 8,\) and \(\overline{AC}\) and \(\overline{BE}\) intersect at \(D.\) What is the difference between the areas of \(\triangle ADE\) and \(\triangle BDC?\)

[Figure 1](figures/2004_AMC_12A_Q08_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The useful observation is that both requested triangles can be obtained by removing the same triangle. Write \([XYZ]\) for the area of \(\triangle XYZ\). Since \(D\) lies on \(BE\), triangle \(ABE\) splits into \(ABD\) and \(ADE\). Since \(D\) also lies on \(AC\), triangle \(ABC\) splits into \(ABD\) and \(BDC\). Subtracting the two area equations cancels \([ABD]\), giving
\[
[ADE]-[BDC]=[ABE]-[ABC].
\]
The given right angles make \(AE=8\) and \(BC=6\) perpendicular heights for the common base \(AB=4\). Thus
\[
[ADE]-[BDC]
=\frac12(4)(8)-\frac12(4)(6)
=4.
\]
This is positive, so \(\triangle ADE\) is larger. The required difference is \(\boxed{4}\), choice \(\mathrm{B}\).
